definition: A graph G = (V, E) consists of a set V of vertices (nodes) and a set E of edges, where each edge connects two vertices. An undirected graph has unordered edges {u,v}; a directed graph (digraph) has ordered edges (u,v). A simple graph has no self-loops or parallel edges. Graphs are the fundamental combinatorial structure for modeling pairwise relations.

contrasts.differential: A graph captures pairwise relations (edges between 2 vertices); a simplicial complex captures higher-order relations (simplices of arbitrary dimension)
A graph has edges connecting exactly 2 vertices; a hypergraph has hyperedges connecting any number of vertices

definition: A vertex (or node) is a fundamental element of a graph. The set of vertices V together with the edge set E defines the graph G = (V, E). The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it. In a directed graph, in-degree counts incoming edges and out-degree counts outgoing edges.

contrasts.differential: Vertices are the atomic elements; edges are the connections between vertices. A graph is defined by both together

definition: An edge connects two vertices in a graph. In an undirected graph, an edge {u,v} is an unordered pair. In a directed graph, an edge (u,v) is an ordered pair (arc) from u to v. Edges may carry weights (weighted graph) or labels. The number of edges is denoted |E| or m.

contrasts.differential: Edges connect vertices; vertices are the elements being connected
An edge connects two adjacent vertices; a path is a sequence of edges connecting a start vertex to an end vertex

definition: A directed graph (digraph) G = (V, E) has edges (arcs) that are ordered pairs (u,v), indicating direction from u to v. Key concepts: in-degree (number of incoming edges), out-degree (number of outgoing edges), strongly connected components, topological ordering (for DAGs). Directed graphs model asymmetric relations like dependencies, causal chains, and information flow.

contrasts.differential: Directed edges have orientation (u->v is different from v->u); undirected edges have no orientation ({u,v} = {v,u})
A directed graph may contain cycles; a DAG (directed acyclic graph) specifically has no directed cycles

definition: A directed acyclic graph: a directed graph with no directed cycles. DAGs admit topological ordering — a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge (u,v), u appears before v. DAGs model dependency structures, partial orders, and computation flows. Every DAG has at least one source (in-degree 0) and at least one sink (out-degree 0).

contrasts.differential: All DAGs are directed graphs but not conversely — directed graphs may contain cycles
Trees are special DAGs where each node has at most one parent. DAGs allow nodes to have multiple parents (shared dependencies)

definition: In graph theory, a cycle is a closed path where no vertex is repeated (except start = end). A graph with no cycles is called acyclic (a forest if undirected, a DAG if directed). The cycle space is the vector space spanned by the independent cycles; its dimension is the circuit rank m - n + c. In directed graphs, a directed cycle follows edge orientations.

contrasts.differential: A path has distinct start and end vertices; a cycle is a closed path (start = end)
Trees are connected acyclic graphs; adding any edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle

definition: A strongly connected component (SCC) of a directed graph G is a maximal subgraph in which every vertex is reachable from every other vertex via directed paths. The SCCs partition the vertices of G. Contracting each SCC to a single vertex yields the condensation — always a DAG. Tarjan's algorithm finds all SCCs in linear time O(V+E).

contrasts.differential: Connected components are for undirected graphs (ignoring edge direction); strongly connected components are for directed graphs (respecting edge direction)
Weakly connected components ignore edge directions; strongly connected components require directed reachability in both directions

definition: The circuit rank (cyclomatic number) of an undirected graph: r = m - n + c, where m = edges, n = vertices, c = connected components. It equals the minimum number of edges to remove to make the graph acyclic, the dimension of the cycle space, and the first Betti number b_1. Introduced by Kirchhoff. For directed graphs, 'cycle rank' can also refer to a different measure of nesting depth of cycles.

contrasts.differential: For graphs, cycle rank = first Betti number b_1. For higher-dimensional complexes, Betti numbers generalize cycle rank
Cycle rank counts the number of independent cycles; girth is the length of the shortest cycle

definition: Two vertices u and v in a graph are adjacent if there is an edge connecting them. The adjacency matrix A of a graph G with n vertices is the n x n matrix where A[i,j] = 1 if vertices i and j are adjacent, 0 otherwise. For weighted graphs, A[i,j] = weight of edge. The adjacency matrix encodes the complete structure of the graph.

contrasts.differential: Adjacency is between two vertices connected by an edge; incidence is between a vertex and an edge containing it

definition: The degree of a vertex v in an undirected graph is the number of edges incident to v, denoted deg(v). In a directed graph: in-degree = number of incoming edges, out-degree = number of outgoing edges. The degree sequence of a graph is the list of all vertex degrees. The handshaking lemma: sum of all degrees = 2|E|.

contrasts.differential: Degree counts the number of adjacent vertices; adjacency is the binary relation of whether two vertices are connected
Degree is a property of a single vertex; degree distribution P(k) gives the fraction of vertices with degree k across the whole graph

definition: A path in a graph is a sequence of distinct vertices v_0, v_1, ..., v_k where each consecutive pair (v_i, v_{i+1}) is connected by an edge. The length of a path is the number of edges (k). A shortest path between two vertices determines the distance between them. In directed graphs, a directed path follows edge orientations.

contrasts.differential: A walk allows repeated vertices and edges; a path requires all vertices to be distinct
A path has distinct start and end; a cycle is a closed path (start = end, with all internal vertices distinct)

definition: A walk in a graph is a sequence of vertices v_0, v_1, ..., v_k where each consecutive pair is connected by an edge, allowing repeated vertices and edges. A closed walk starts and ends at the same vertex. A walk with no repeated edges is a trail; a walk with no repeated vertices is a path.

contrasts.differential: A walk allows vertex repetition; a path requires all vertices to be distinct
A walk allows edge repetition; a trail requires all edges to be distinct

definition: A connected acyclic undirected graph. Equivalently: a connected graph with |V|-1 edges, or a graph where there is exactly one path between any two vertices. Trees are the minimally connected graphs. A rooted tree has a designated root vertex; a forest is an acyclic graph (union of trees). Every connected graph has a spanning tree.

contrasts.differential: A tree is connected; a forest is a disjoint union of trees (connected acyclic components)
Trees have exactly one path between any two vertices; DAGs may have multiple directed paths between vertices

definition: An acyclic undirected graph, i.e., a disjoint union of trees. A forest with n vertices and c connected components has exactly n - c edges. A spanning forest of a graph G is a maximal acyclic subgraph — it contains all vertices and n - c edges, where c is the number of connected components of G.

contrasts.differential: A tree is a connected forest (single component); a forest may have multiple components
A spanning tree exists only for connected graphs; a spanning forest is the generalization for disconnected graphs

definition: A spanning tree of a connected graph G is a subgraph that is a tree and includes all vertices of G. It has exactly |V|-1 edges. The edges not in a spanning tree are called chords or back edges; each chord creates exactly one fundamental cycle. The number of chords equals the cycle rank r = |E| - |V| + 1.

contrasts.differential: A spanning tree is any tree subgraph including all vertices; a minimum spanning tree minimizes the sum of edge weights
A BFS tree is a specific spanning tree built by breadth-first search; spanning trees in general can have any structure

definition: Tarjan's algorithm finds all strongly connected components (SCCs) of a directed graph in linear time O(V+E) using a single depth-first search. It maintains a stack of vertices and assigns each vertex a discovery index and a low-link value. A vertex v is the root of an SCC iff its low-link equals its discovery index; at that point, all vertices above v on the stack form the SCC. Introduced by Robert Tarjan (1972).

contrasts.differential: Both find SCCs in O(V+E), but Kosaraju requires two DFS passes; Tarjan uses one pass with a stack
Tarjan's algorithm can produce a reverse topological ordering of the SCC condensation as a byproduct; topological sort orders vertices in a DAG

definition: A probability distribution P(k) ~ k^{-gamma} where the probability decreases as a power of k. In network science, a degree distribution following a power law indicates a scale-free network: many low-degree nodes and few high-degree hubs. Most real-world scale-free networks have exponents 2 < gamma < 3. Power laws appear in city sizes, word frequencies, wealth distributions, and many natural phenomena.

contrasts.differential: Normal distributions have a characteristic scale (mean); power-law distributions are scale-free — no characteristic value dominates
Exponential distributions decay faster than any power law; power laws have heavy tails with significantly more extreme values

definition: A network whose degree distribution follows a power law P(k) ~ k^{-gamma}. Scale-free networks feature a few highly connected hubs and many low-degree nodes. The Barabasi-Albert model generates scale-free networks through preferential attachment (new nodes preferentially connect to already well-connected nodes). Examples: World Wide Web, citation networks, protein interaction networks.

contrasts.differential: Random (Erdos-Renyi) networks have Poisson degree distributions with a characteristic scale; scale-free networks have power-law distributions with no characteristic scale
Regular networks have identical degree for all nodes; scale-free networks have extreme degree heterogeneity

definition: A node with significantly higher degree than most other nodes in a network. In scale-free networks, hubs arise naturally from preferential attachment — 'the rich get richer.' Hubs are critical for network connectivity: removing a few hubs can fragment the network (vulnerability to targeted attack), while random node removal has little effect (robustness to random failure).

contrasts.differential: A hub has very high degree; a leaf has degree 1 (connected to only one other node)
In a scale-free network, most nodes are 'average' with few connections; hubs are the rare high-degree outliers
